title: Dangerous Calling
subtitle: Why the Office of Pastor Is Not for Everyone
blurb: The office of pastor is not a career, a platform, or a reward for being good with words. It is a weight God lays on a particular kind of person and refuses to lay on most. This book argues, without softening the edge, that some should not enter the office, that the qualifications God screens for are matters of character before competence, and that the calling, when it is real, costs more than anyone tells you and is worth more than anything you gave up.

chapters.title: The Weight Nobody Warned You About
chapters.summary: Pastoral ministry is presented as opportunity when Scripture presents it as weight. This chapter names the gap between the romance of the office and the burden of it.
chapters.body:
The first thing the New Testament says about the desire to be a pastor is that it is a good thing to desire. The second thing it says is that almost no one should do it. We quote the first verse on the recruitment posters. We bury the second one.

"If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task" (1 Timothy 3:1). And then, a different writer, plainer and harder: "Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness" (James 3:1). Both are true. They are meant to be held together, the way a man holds a hot coal and a clean cup in the same hands and does not confuse them. The church has spent a generation holding only the cup.

I came to faith out of atheism. I was not raised in a sanctuary; I argued against the people who were. So when I finally walked into ministry I did not come carrying the inherited assumption that the pastorate was a respectable Christian profession, the way a doctor's son assumes medicine. I came carrying nothing but the shock of having been wrong about God. And what struck me first, once I started reading the men who had actually done this work, was how frightened the best of them were. Not anxious. Frightened. Augustine wept when the church at Hippo seized him and demanded he be ordained. Gregory the Great called the pastoral office *ars artium*, the art of arts, the government of souls, and he called himself a fraud for accepting it. These were not weak men. They were men who had counted the weight and found it nearly unbearable.

We do not raise pastors that way anymore. We raise them on opportunity. We tell a gifted young man that he has a "gift for communication" and that there is a "great need," and we move him toward a stage, and we measure his readiness by how the room responds to him. The room responding is the most dangerous data a young man can be handed. It tells him nothing about whether he can carry a dying woman's family through the worst Tuesday of their lives. It tells him only that he is pleasant to listen to. Spurgeon, lecturing his students in London in the 1870s, warned them against exactly this: the ministry as a thing the man performs rather than a thing the man is.

Here is what nobody warned me about. The weight is not the sermon. The sermon is the visible part, the part the world grades. The weight is the eleven o'clock phone call. The weight is the elder whose marriage you have watched curdle for two years and cannot fix. The weight is knowing things about people in your congregation that you will carry, alone, in silence, until you die, because to speak them would be a second betrayal. The weight is standing over a casket the size of a shoebox and being expected to say something true about God while the parents look at you, and meaning it, and not knowing if you do. That is the office. The stage is the smallest room in the house.

Eugene Peterson spent his life trying to pull pastors back from the idea that they were running a religious business. He kept insisting the work was small, slow, local, unglamorous: this town, these people, this Bible, over years. The American instinct is to scale. The pastoral vocation does not scale. A soul is cared for one at a time or it is not cared for. You cannot mass-produce a deathbed. You cannot delegate the moment a teenager tells you he no longer believes any of it and is watching your face to see if you flinch.

So before we talk about qualifications, before Timothy and Titus, before the temptations and the glory, I want to set the weight down in front of you and ask you to look at it. Not to admire it. To feel its mass.

Because the tragedy of the modern church is not that too few want the office. The tragedy is that too many want it for reasons that have nothing to do with the office. They want to be heard. They want to matter. They want the affirmation of standing in front of a room and being received as wise. These are not evil desires. They are human desires. But they are not a call. A call is when God lays the weight on you and you find, to your own surprise, that you would rather die under it than put it down.

I have known men who wanted to be pastors the way a boy wants to be an astronaut. The wanting was real. It was also entirely about the launch and not at all about the long cold dark of the actual flight. When the launch faded, when the novelty of the role wore off and what remained was the daily grind of loving difficult people who would not love them back the way they had imagined, those men left. Not because they failed. Because they were never carrying the weight in the first place. They were carrying the image of themselves carrying the weight. There is a difference, and the difference is everything.

I am inside this indictment. I have wanted to be heard. I have stood in a pulpit on a morning when my own faith was hanging by a thread and felt the warm approval of a room and let it stand in, for a moment, where God should have been. Any honest pastor has done this. The question is not whether you are tempted by the romance of the office. You will be. The question is whether the romance is the thing holding you, or whether underneath it there is something heavier and quieter that will hold when the romance is gone.

Bonhoeffer wrote that when Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die. He meant every Christian. He meant it doubly for those who would lead. The pastorate is not the exemption from that death. It is its intensification, lived in public, where everyone can watch you fail to do it well.

I am not trying to talk you out of it. If God has called you, nothing I write could talk you out of it, and nothing the world offers could keep you in it. I am trying to make you feel the mass of the thing before you pick it up. Because a man who picks up a weight he has correctly measured can carry it for forty years. A man who picks up a weight he thought was lighter drops it in year three, and the people underneath him are crushed.

Set it down in front of you. Look at it. Do not pick it up yet.
chapters.verdict: The office is not a door you walk through. It is a yoke you carry.
reflect: When you picture yourself as a pastor, do you picture the platform or the weight?
What is it you actually want when you want this office?
Have you ever sat with the possibility that wanting it is not the same as being made for it?

chapters.title: Not Everyone Is Called, and That Is Mercy
chapters.summary: The democratization of calling has erased a biblical distinction; not everyone is called to teach, and the limit is a kindness, not an insult.
chapters.body:
We have made calling a democracy. Everyone is called. Calling has become the Christian word for "wants to," dressed up so it cannot be questioned. To tell a man he may not be called is now heard as an insult, a rejection of his worth, an act of gatekeeping by the threatened. And so we have stopped saying it. We let men ordain themselves on the strength of their enthusiasm, and we are surprised, three years later, by the wreckage.

"Not many of you should become teachers" (James 3:1). The verse is not difficult. It is unwelcome. It assumes a category of person who wants the office but should not have it, and it addresses them directly, and it tells them no. We do not preach this verse. We cannot. Our whole culture of affirmation forbids it. The one passage that screens people out of the office has been quietly retired from the conversation about who should enter the office.

I want to say something that will sound harsh and is in fact the kindest thing in this book. Not everyone is called. The closed door is mercy.

Think about what we do when we tell every eager young man that he is called. We take a man whose gifts lie elsewhere, whose temperament will be torn apart by the work, whose marriage will not survive the schedule, whose pride will be inflamed rather than humbled by the platform, and we hand him a yoke built for a different animal. And then, when he breaks, we say he "burned out," as though the office were a furnace and not a fit. He did not burn out. He was placed where he was never meant to stand, by people who could not bring themselves to tell him the truth, because telling the truth felt unkind. The unkindness was the affirmation.

The Reformers, recovering the priesthood of all believers, never meant to erase the distinction between the general call of every Christian to ministry and the particular call to the office of elder. Every believer is a priest. Not every believer is a pastor. Luther held both. The flattening of these two into one — the idea that because all are ministers, all who wish may hold the office — is a modern confusion that would have baffled the very men who recovered the doctrine. The priesthood of all believers exalts the layperson. It does not lower the bar for the elder.

Consider what the call actually is, biblically. It is not a feeling. Feelings lie, and they lie most loudly to the men most desperate to be told they are special. The call is a convergence: an internal desire, yes (1 Timothy 3:1), but tested against an external recognition by a community that knows you, measured against a list of qualifications that are almost entirely about character, and confirmed by actual fruit in the actual lives of actual people. When all of these converge, you may begin to suspect a call. When only the internal desire is present, you have a feeling. We have built an entire pipeline that runs on the feeling and skips the rest.

I have had to tell men no. It is among the hardest things I do, and the most important. A man sits across from me, sincere, gifted in some ways, on fire to enter the ministry, and everything in me wants to bless it, because the room of the heart leans toward yes, and because no feels like a judgment on his soul. But I have watched what happens when the wrong man is told yes by someone too cowardly to say no. The damage is not abstract. It is a congregation split. It is a family in another state who trusted their daughter to a man who should never have held authority. It is the man himself, twenty years later, bitter and hollow, having spent his life proving he belonged in a place he was never built for. The kind thing, the only kind thing, was the hard word early.

And here is the part that the man being told no cannot see in the moment, and that I beg you to see now if you are reading this and afraid the door might be closing. A no from God to this office is not a no to you. It is not a demotion in the kingdom. The kingdom does not run on a hierarchy with pastors at the top. That is a lie the office itself whispers to the men inside it, and it has damned more than a few of them. The mother raising children in the faith, the man who runs an honest business with an open hand, the widow who prays, the believer who simply lives the ordinary obedient life with joy — these are not the junior varsity of the church. The pastorate is a function, not a rank. To be denied a function is not to be denied your standing before God, which was settled at the cross and cannot be added to by ordination or subtracted from by its absence.

Bonhoeffer wrote that the man who loves his dream of community more than the community itself destroys the community, even when his intentions are honest. The same is true of the man who loves his dream of being a pastor more than he loves the people a pastor exists to serve. He will sacrifice the real church on the altar of his imagined role. And so the church's refusal to hand him the role is not cruelty toward him. It is protection of the flock from him, and, if he could see it, protection of him from himself.

I say this as a man who was, by every reasonable measure, the wrong candidate. An atheist. No father in the home to model what a steady man even looked like. Nothing in my background that recommended me for the care of souls. If calling were a meritocracy, I would have been screened out, and rightly. That God called me anyway is not evidence that calling is open to all. It is evidence that the One who calls is not bound by our resumes — which is a different thing entirely, and not a loophole anyone can claim for himself.

So receive the no, if it comes, as the word of a God who loves you too much to place you where you would be destroyed. And receive the yes, if it is real, as a summons to die, not a promotion to a better seat. Either way, the question was never whether you wanted it. The question was always whether you were given it. Those are not the same. Confusing them has ruined men I have loved.
chapters.verdict: A door God has closed to you is not a wound. It is protection.
reflect: Have you treated "called" as a status you are entitled to rather than a summons you must receive?
Whose discernment about your fitness have you refused to hear?
If God said no to this office, would your faith survive it?

chapters.title: Character Before Competence
chapters.summary: The qualification lists in 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 screen almost entirely for character, not skill; the church has reversed the order.
chapters.body:
Read the qualifications for an elder and notice what is almost entirely absent. "An overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money" (1 Timothy 3:2-3). Titus repeats and sharpens it: "not arrogant, not quick-tempered... but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined" (Titus 1:7-8). Run your eye down the list. Twelve, fifteen marks of character. One, exactly one, mark of competence: able to teach. And even that is not "gifted to teach" or "compelling to listen to." It is *able* — sound enough in doctrine and clear enough in speech to hand on what was received.

The list is a character screen. We have turned it into a competence screen. This is the central inversion of pastoral selection in our time, and almost everything that goes wrong downstream begins here.

Watch how a church actually hires a pastor. It watches him preach. It checks his references, which mostly speak to whether people liked working with him. It looks at the numbers from his last post — did the church grow, did giving rise, did the young families come. It runs him through an interview where he performs warmth and theological fluency for ninety minutes. And then it calls him. At no point in this process does anyone live with the man for the months it would take to learn whether he is gentle when no one is watching, whether he is quick-tempered with his wife, whether he loves money, whether he is hospitable when it costs him, whether he is the same man at home that he is on the platform. The very things Paul says to screen for are the things our process cannot see. The very thing Paul mentions almost in passing — ability to teach — is the only thing our process measures.

The result is predictable and we see it constantly. Men of immense competence and hollow character rise, because the system rewards the visible and cannot detect the invisible. And the rot, when it surfaces, surfaces as scandal, and we say we are shocked. We are not entitled to be shocked. We built a selection process that screens for exactly the wrong thing and then we express dismay when it delivers exactly what it was designed to deliver.

Richard Baxter, the Puritan pastor of Kidderminster, wrote in *The Reformed Pastor* in 1656 a sentence that every man entering this office should have to copy out by hand: take heed to yourselves before you take heed to the flock. He saw that a man cannot give what he does not have, cannot lead where he has not gone, cannot tend in others a garden he has let go to weeds in himself. Baxter was relentless on this. The minister's own soul is the first parish. Neglect it and every other parish you touch is contaminated by the neglect.

Here is the subtle danger, and I have felt it in my own bones. Competence can substitute for character so smoothly that the man himself cannot tell the difference. A gifted preacher can preach a sermon on humility that moves a thousand people while being, himself, a proud man, and the gift will carry the sermon, and the people will be genuinely fed, and the man will conclude from the feeding that he must be humble, because look at the fruit. The gift becomes the evidence of the godliness it is actually concealing. This is the most dangerous trap in the office, because it is invisible from the inside. The better you are at the work, the more cover your gifts provide for the state of your soul, and the less anyone — including you — looks underneath.

Character before competence does not mean competence does not matter. A man who cannot teach should not be an elder; the office requires it. But the order is the whole point. Character is the foundation; competence is the structure built on it. Build the structure on no foundation and the more impressive the structure, the more catastrophic the eventual collapse. We are living through a season of collapses. The buildings were impressive. There was nothing underneath.

What does it mean, practically, to screen for character? It means time. There is no shortcut. You cannot assess "above reproach" in an interview; you can only assess it across years, in the testimony of people who have seen the man under pressure, in private, in the small decisions that no one celebrates and everyone reveals themselves by. Paul tells Timothy not to be hasty in laying on hands (1 Timothy 5:22), and the haste he warns against is precisely our haste, the rush to fill a pulpit, the eagerness to deploy a promising man before his character has been tested. "He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit" (1 Timothy 3:6). Time is not a bureaucratic obstacle to ordination. Time is the test itself. Pride needs no incubation; it is the default. Only time, and trial, and the slow accountability of a community, reveals whether grace has done its deeper work or merely decorated the surface.

I think often about the men I have watched fall. In almost every case, the gifts were never in question. The man could preach. The man could lead. The man could build. What was in question, always, was the thing no one had taken the time to examine: whether the private man matched the public one. And in almost every case, the people who knew him most closely — a wife, an associate, an elder who had seen too much — had known the answer for years and had not been asked, or had been asked and not believed, because the gifts were so loud they drowned out the testimony.

God screens for who you are. He has always screened for who you are. He chose a murderer named Moses and a coward named Gideon and a denier named Peter, and what He did with each of them first, before any deployment, was take them into the wilderness and break the man underneath until the gift had something true to rest on. The wilderness is not a detour on the way to the office. The wilderness is the qualification. Skip it, and you will be qualified for the platform and disqualified for the soul.
chapters.verdict: God ordains who a man is. The church too often ordains what a man can do.
reflect: If your private character were the only qualification, would you be ordained?
Which of the qualities in 1 Timothy 3 are you quietly hoping no one examines?
Have you mistaken your gifting for your godliness?

chapters.title: The Public Self That Outruns the Private One
chapters.summary: The peculiar temptation of the office is to let the constructed public self grow larger and truer than the private man, until the gap becomes a fault line.
chapters.body:
Every pastor builds two men. There is the man who stands up front, composed, articulate, spiritually weighty, the man the congregation knows and trusts and to some degree needs. And there is the man who lies awake at two in the morning, who is short with his children, who has private doubts and private appetites and a private cowardice he has shown no one. The first man is not a lie, exactly. He is real, on the platform, for that hour. But he is a construction, assembled for public use. The danger of the office is that the public man can grow faster, and stand taller, and become more convincing — even to the pastor himself — than the private man underneath. And the gap between them becomes the place where ministries die.

This is the temptation peculiar to the office. The accountant does not face it; no one is watching his soul for inspiration. But the pastor's very job requires him to embody what he proclaims, to stand as a kind of living exhibit of the life he commends. And so he is under constant pressure to perform a self that is further along than he actually is. The pressure is not entirely external. A congregation does need its pastor to be, in some sense, ahead of them. But the pastor learns to manage the gap by managing the appearance, and the management of appearance is a skill, and like all skills it improves with practice, until he is very, very good at seeming, and the seeming has quietly replaced the being.

Spurgeon warned his students that a minister could spend so long preparing food for others that he starved himself, handling holy things until they became merely professional, the Bible a quarry for sermons rather than the voice of God to his own soul. This is the mechanism. The pastor's spiritual life becomes occupational. He reads Scripture for material. He prays in public with fluency and in private barely at all. He counsels others toward intimacy with God while his own intimacy with God has curdled into expertise about God. And no one can tell, because the public output is undiminished. The sermons are still good. The prayers still move people. The machine runs beautifully on the fumes of a tank that emptied years ago.

I know this temptation from the inside, and I will not pretend otherwise. There have been seasons when I was more diligent about how I appeared to my congregation than about how I appeared to God, when my reputation got more of my attention than my conscience. The platform rewards this. The platform cannot see your prayer closet. It can only see your performance, and it applauds the performance, and the applause is sincere, and the applause is the very thing slowly killing the man who receives it. Augustine, in the *Confessions*, was savage with himself on this point — the desire to be praised, the way it followed him even into his religion, the way it could colonize even his repentance, so that he found himself proud of his humility. He understood that the love of praise is not a sin the pastor leaves behind at the door. It is the sin that waits for him inside, in the holiest room, dressed as ministry.

Here is the diagnostic. The distance between your public self and your private self is the exact measure of your spiritual danger. Not the size of your platform. Not the scale of your ministry. The gap. A man with a small ministry and no gap is safe. A man with a vast ministry and a vast gap is a building already on fire; the only question is when the smoke reaches the windows. And the cruelty of the gap is that the larger your platform grows, the more your private self is tempted to atrophy, because the public rewards keep flowing regardless, and the human heart does not maintain what it is not forced to maintain.

What closes the gap? Not trying harder to be good in public. That only widens it, because it pours more energy into the performance. The gap closes only by deliberately building a life in private that no one will ever see — secret obedience, secret prayer, secret generosity, secret confession of secret sin to one or two people who know the whole man and love him anyway. Jesus was direct about this: "when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret" (Matthew 6:6). The secret room is not a nice spiritual extra for the pastor. It is the only place the private man gets fed, and a private man who is not fed will eventually be eaten by the public man, and the public man, having consumed the private one, becomes a hollow and dangerous thing wearing a pastor's face.

The whitewashed tomb was Jesus' image for it (Matthew 23:27). Beautiful on the outside. Full of death within. He aimed it at the most religious, most respected, most publicly impressive men of his day — not at the obvious sinners, but at the professionals of righteousness whose public selves had outrun their private ones by a country mile. It is the most frightening passage in the Gospels for anyone who stands up front for a living, because it describes a condition that is invisible to the man who has it and visible to God alone, and it pronounces over that condition not a warning but a woe.

I have a practice I commend, and I try, imperfectly, to keep it. Once in a while, do something genuinely good that no one will ever find out about. Give where it cannot be traced. Serve where you will not be thanked. Confess where it costs your image. Not as a technique — God is not fooled by techniques — but as a way of feeding the private man, of insisting that he keep growing, of refusing to let the public construction become the only self you have. The goal is not to be impressive in secret. The goal is to be the same man in both rooms, so that one day, when the platform is gone and only the private man remains, there is still a man there at all.

Most of the falls you have read about were not sudden. They were the day the gap, grown too wide to hold, finally tore. The fall was visible. The tearing had been going on for years, in private, where no one was watching, which was exactly the point.
chapters.verdict: The distance between your platform and your prayer closet is the exact measure of your danger.
reflect: How wide is the gap between the man your congregation sees and the man your spouse lives with?
When did you last do something good that no one would ever know about?
Are you more careful about your reputation than your conscience?

chapters.title: Ambition Baptized
chapters.summary: The office gives ambition a holy disguise; the desire to build God's kingdom and the desire to build your own become nearly indistinguishable.
chapters.body:
Ambition is not the obvious sin in the pastorate. It is the disguised one. In any other field a man's drive to grow his enterprise is named for what it is. In ministry, the same drive gets baptized. We call it vision. We call it a heart for the lost. We call it stewardship of the gifts God gave. And sometimes it is those things. But the human heart is an expert at routing self-interest through the language of self-denial, and nowhere does it have a richer vocabulary to route it through than in the work of God.

Consider how seamlessly the two ambitions merge. A pastor wants his church to grow. This is, on its face, holy — more people hearing the gospel, more souls cared for. But a growing church also means a larger platform for the pastor, a bigger budget, more invitations to speak, a rising reputation, the quiet thrill of being the man whose ministry is going somewhere. The kingdom's interest and the pastor's interest run in parallel for a long stretch, close enough that the man himself cannot tell which one he is actually serving. And because he cannot tell, he assumes the holy one, because that is the assumption that lets him keep his self-image intact. This is ambition baptized: self-promotion that has learned to dress as kingdom work and even to fool the man wearing the costume.

James saw this clearly and named it with a precision that should make every ministry leader flinch: "where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice" (James 3:16). Notice that it sits a few verses after "not many of you should become teachers." James connects them. The teacher's peculiar danger is the ambition that hides inside the teaching office, because the office offers ambition such a perfect camouflage. Jesus' own disciples argued about who was greatest (Mark 9:34) — while following the Messiah, on the road, in the middle of the most important ministry in human history. If they could do it there, do not imagine you are immune in your far smaller theater.

The test of ambition is obscurity. Not failure — obscurity. Could you do this work, faithfully, joyfully, for forty years, in a place no one would ever hear of, shepherding people no conference would ever invite you to speak about, with no growing platform, no book deal, no rising profile, nothing but the slow holy work of one town and one Bible and these particular people? If the answer is no — if the thought of permanent obscurity drains the joy out of the calling — then it was never the calling you loved. It was the trajectory. And a man who loves the trajectory will, sooner or later, sacrifice the people to protect it.

Eugene Peterson spent decades hammering this, against the entire current of American church culture. He insisted that the pastoral vocation is not a career with a ladder, that the relentless drive toward bigger and more is a worldly ambition wearing a clerical collar, and that the faithful pastor must resist it the way an addict resists a drug, because it is exactly that seductive and exactly that destructive. He chose a small church. He stayed. He resisted every pull toward scale. And he was treated, by much of the church-growth movement, as a quaint underachiever — which tells you everything about how thoroughly the church has internalized the world's definition of a successful ministry.

I have felt the pull, and I will name it, because to pretend otherwise would be its own performance. I founded a network of pastors. The mission is real; the need is real; pastors are isolated and dying and need each other. But I would be a liar if I told you the network has never also been a place where my own name grows, where my reach extends, where the line between serving pastors and being the man who serves pastors blurs past my ability to see it. The two ambitions run in parallel in me as in everyone. I do not get to stand outside this and diagnose it in you. I am inside it. The most I can do is keep asking the question and keep distrusting my own quick answer.

The deadliest form of this is the decision that serves the kingdom and conveniently also serves you, and you make it, and you tell yourself you made it for the kingdom, and there is no one in the room who can prove otherwise, including your own conscience. The new building that the ministry needs and that also becomes your monument. The expansion that reaches more people and also enlarges your domain. The hard stand on principle that is genuinely principled and also, not coincidentally, raises your profile among the people whose approval you crave. These are not hypocritical decisions. They are mixed ones, and the mixture is the danger, because the holy part provides perfect cover for the part that is not.

What is the remedy? Not the renunciation of all desire to grow; that is a false and impossible piety, and it often masks a different ambition, the ambition to be seen as the humble one. The remedy is brutal honesty about the mixture, sustained over years, with people who are not impressed by you and will not let you get away with the holy version of the story. The remedy is to regularly choose the obscure good over the visible one, the small faithfulness over the large recognition, on purpose, as a discipline, to keep the muscle of self-denial from atrophying. The remedy is to genuinely rejoice when another man's ministry grows and yours does not, and to watch your own reaction to his growth as the most honest measurement available of where your heart actually is. Your envy of another pastor's success will tell you more about your soul than any amount of introspection, because envy does not lie. It surfaces the ambition the language had been hiding.

John the Baptist watched his entire ministry drain away to a younger man and said, "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30). He said it as joy, not defeat. That sentence is the death of baptized ambition, and almost no one in the office can say it and mean it. I cannot, most days. But the days I can are the only days I am safe.
chapters.verdict: The most dangerous ambition is the kind you have learned to call obedience.
reflect: When your church grows, who are you actually pleased for?
Could you serve faithfully in a place no one would ever hear of?
Have you ever made a "kingdom" decision that conveniently also enlarged you?

chapters.title: The Loneliness of the Set-Apart
chapters.summary: The office isolates by its nature; the pastor is in the congregation but cannot be fully of it, and the loneliness becomes a doorway to ruin if not understood.
chapters.body:
The pastor is surrounded by people and is profoundly alone. This is not a complaint; it is a structural feature of the office, and the man who does not understand it will be destroyed by it without ever knowing what hit him. He is in the congregation but cannot be wholly of it. He knows everyone's secrets and can share none of his own. He is the one others come to in crisis, and when his own crisis comes, the people he would naturally turn to are the very people he must not burden, because he is their pastor, and a pastor who collapses onto his congregation has inverted the order of care and frightened the flock.

The loneliness is real and it is peculiar. A friend can tell his friends he is struggling. The pastor's struggles are, to his congregation, a kind of betrayal of the role — not because they are unkind, but because they need him to be standing when they cannot. The man who counsels the grieving has his own griefs. The man who absorbs the anxiety of a hundred families carries it home and has nowhere to set it down, because the natural place to set it down is the home and the marriage that are already carrying more than their share of the cost of his calling. So he carries it alone. And carrying it alone, year after year, is how the strongest men I know became the most vulnerable.

Listen to where the falls actually come from. Ask the men who fell, in the honest aftermath, and you will rarely hear "I stopped believing the doctrine." You will hear, in some form, "I was alone." The affair began as a conversation with the one person who seemed to see the man and not the office. The drinking began as the only way to set the weight down at the end of a day that no one else could share. The financial sin began in a secrecy that had become the man's native air, because secrecy was the medium he had lived in for twenty years. Isolation is not the fall. Isolation is the soil the fall grows in, and the office tills that soil daily.

Bonhoeffer wrote, in *Life Together*, that the pious community can be the deadliest place to be alone, because there everyone is expected to be strong, and the sin no one can confess festers in a way it never would among honest sinners who knew themselves to be such. He understood that the demand for spiritual strength, when it forbids the admission of weakness, drives weakness underground, where it grows in the dark. The pastor lives at the center of exactly this demand. He is the one most expected to be strong, and therefore the one most forbidden to confess, and therefore the one most exposed to the slow rot of the unconfessed.

Here is the structural problem laid bare. The pastor often has no one above him and no one beside him. No one above: in many churches he is the final authority, the man who answers to a board he in practice leads and a denomination he rarely sees. No one beside: his staff report to him, his elders depend on him, his congregation looks up to him, and so every relationship in his life runs vertically, with him at the top, and a man at the top of every relationship he has is a man no one can correct. Jesus sent the disciples out two by two (Mark 6:7). Paul traveled with Barnabas, then Silas, then a whole company. The New Testament does not imagine the solitary leader. We have built it anyway, and we are paying for it in a long parade of men who had everything except a single human being who could tell them no.

I have had to fight for this in my own life, and I do not always win. The pull toward isolation is not laziness; it is the gravity of the office itself. It is easier, in the short run, to carry it alone than to make yourself known to someone who could see your weakness and think less of you. Founding the Pastors Connection Network was, among other things, an attempt to build for other men the thing the office systematically denies them: a place where a pastor can stop being the strong one for an hour and be, simply, a man who is not okay, among other men who are not okay, none of whom report to him. The need for such a place is itself the indictment. That it has to be deliberately constructed tells you how thoroughly the office isolates by default.

What does the answer look like? It is not more friends in the congregation, though that has its place. It is, specifically, relationships outside the lines of authority — men who do not attend your church, cannot benefit from your favor, cannot be harmed by your displeasure, and therefore have no reason to flatter you and every freedom to tell you the truth. You need at least one person who knows the whole truth about you, including the parts you would be ashamed for your congregation to learn, and who is not impressed by your office, and whom you cannot fire, ignore, or out-rank. If no such person exists in your life, understand clearly what your situation is. You are not safe and strong. You are alone and falling. You have simply not yet landed.

"Two are better than one... For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up" (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10). Woe. The same word Jesus used over the whitewashed tombs. The Preacher is not offering relationship advice. He is pronouncing a verdict over the solitary man, and the pastor, by the structure of his office, is the solitary man par excellence unless he fights, hard and against the grain, to be otherwise.

The set-apart life is real. Paul was set apart for the gospel (Romans 1:1), and there is a holy separateness to the office that cannot be erased without erasing the office. But set apart was never meant to mean alone. The first community God called out called itself out together. The man who reads his ordination as a vow of solitary strength has misread it, and the misreading will cost him everything, and worse, it will cost the people who trusted that the strong man up front was actually as strong as he seemed.
chapters.verdict: A pastor who has no one above him and no one beside him is already falling; he simply has not landed yet.
reflect: Who knows the whole truth about you, including what you would be ashamed for your church to know?
Have you confused being surrounded by people with being known?
Is there anyone in your life you cannot fire, ignore, or out-rank?

chapters.title: When the Gift Becomes the Idol
chapters.summary: A pastor's gifts can become the thing he worships and the thing that destroys him, precisely because they are genuine and God-given.
chapters.body:
The cruelest trap in the office is set not by a man's sins but by his gifts. We expect to be undone by our weaknesses; we guard against them; we confess them. We do not guard against our strengths, because strengths feel like the safe part, the God-given part, the part that justifies our presence in the office. And so the strength goes unwatched, and the unwatched strength, over years, becomes the idol, and the idol, in the end, becomes the instrument of ruin. The thing that built your ministry is the most likely thing to bury you. I have watched it happen too many times to believe otherwise.

Consider the gifted preacher. His gift is real; God gave it; people are genuinely fed by it. But the gift also delivers a continuous stream of affirmation, week after week, the particular intoxication of holding a room and being received as wise, and the human heart was not built to receive that much approval without being warped by it. Slowly, almost invisibly, the gift stops being something the man offers to God and becomes something the man needs from people. He no longer preaches to feed the flock; he preaches to be fed by the response. He cannot tell the difference, because the external act is identical. Only the internal direction has reversed. The gift now points back at him, and he serves it, and it has become his god.

This is idolatry in its most respectable form. The Bible's relentless concern with idolatry is not primarily about statues; it is about the human capacity to take good things and seat them where only God belongs. "They exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images" (Romans 1:23) — and the image a pastor is most tempted to exchange the glory of God for is not carved wood. It is his own gift, his own effectiveness, his own indispensability, the reflected glory of being good at the work of God. The most dangerous idols are the ones made out of genuine blessings, because no one suspects a blessing of being an idol, least of all the man it is blessing.

The diagnostic question is simple and brutal: Do you possess your gifts, or do they possess you? A man who possesses his gifts can imagine losing them and remain himself. A man possessed by his gifts cannot — the loss of the gift would be the loss of the self, because the self has been built on the gift rather than on God. So ask: what would be left of you if it were taken? If the voice failed, the mind dimmed, the platform vanished, the people stopped responding — who would you be? If the honest answer is "no one," then the gift is not your servant. It is your master, and you are worshiping it, and you have made the most respectable possible idol out of the most genuine possible blessing.

There is a darker turn still. A gift, once it has become an idol, will be used in the service of the idol's appetites, which is to say it will be used to obtain ungodly things by godly means. The gifted counselor uses his genuine insight to make a vulnerable person dependent on him. The gifted leader uses his genuine vision to consolidate power he tells himself is for the kingdom. The gifted communicator uses his genuine eloquence to spin a sin into a story that protects him. The gift is real every time. That is what makes it so effective and so damning. Saul prophesied (1 Samuel 19:24) while pursuing David to kill him. Balaam blessed Israel with his mouth while his heart ran after the wages of unrighteousness (2 Peter 2:15). A genuine gift in the service of an ungodly heart is not a contradiction. It is the most common form of the tragedy.

I have to watch this in myself, and the watching is hard precisely because the gift feels like the most reliably good thing about me. When I write, when I teach, when something I say lands and I can see it land in someone's face — there is a pleasure in that which is partly holy and partly poison, and I cannot always separate the two. The pleasure of being used by God and the pleasure of being good at it sit so close together that they share a border I cannot reliably find. To pretend I have mastered this would be to demonstrate that I have not. The man who thinks his gift no longer tempts him toward idolatry is the man the idol has most fully captured, because it has captured even his self-awareness.

What guards against it? First, regular periods of deliberate uselessness — Sabbath, rest, time in which you produce nothing and are valued for nothing and discover whether there is a self there when the gift is set down. The man who cannot rest is the man whose identity has migrated into his output. God commanded the Sabbath partly for this: to break, weekly, the lie that we are what we produce (Exodus 20:8-11). Second, accountability specifically around the gift, not just around the obvious sins. Ask someone to watch not whether you are using your gift, but why — whether the direction has reversed, whether you are starting to need the response more than you serve the people. Third, the willingness to lay the gift down when God or wisdom requires it, to prove to yourself that you can, the way Abraham proved he held Isaac with an open hand by being willing to give him back (Genesis 22).

The gift is good. That is the whole problem. If it were evil you would guard it. Because it is good, you trust it, and you stop watching it, and the unwatched good thing in the heart of a sinful man does not stay good. It grows quietly into the thing he serves, and then into the thing that destroys him, and at the funeral of his ministry everyone says what a gift he had, never suspecting that the gift was the murder weapon.
chapters.verdict: The gift that built your ministry is the most likely thing to bury you.
reflect: Do you possess your gifts, or do they possess you?
What would be left of your sense of self if the gift were taken away?
Have you ever used a genuine spiritual gift to get something ungodly?

chapters.title: The Family You Pastor Last
chapters.summary: The office tempts a man to spend himself on the congregation and starve the family Scripture says he must lead first; how a man manages his own house is itself a qualification.
chapters.body:
Paul slips a strange qualification into the list, and we read past it because it is uncomfortable: an elder "must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?" (1 Timothy 3:4-5). The home is not separate from the qualification for ministry. The home is a qualification for ministry. The way a man leads the small flock God gave him before He gave him any other is the evidence the church is told to examine before trusting him with a larger one. We have decided to treat this as private and off-limits. Paul treats it as the test.

The office tempts a man to invert this with a ferocity that is hard to describe to anyone who has not stood inside it. The congregation's needs are urgent, visible, and endless. They produce gratitude, affirmation, the sense of being needed and effective. The family's needs are chronic, invisible, and unglamorous, and they produce, mostly, no applause at all. A dying member needs you tonight; your son also needs you tonight, but your son will probably still be there next week, and the dying member will not, and so you go, and you go again, and you go for twenty years, and you tell yourself you are choosing the kingdom over your comfort. You are not. You are choosing the visible flock over the invisible one, the applauded service over the unapplauded, and you are calling it sacrifice when it is, too often, the opposite of sacrifice — it is the easier love, the love that pays you back.

This is the part I cannot write about with any distance, and I will not pretend to. I have five sons. I was raised without a father, which means I came into fatherhood with no map, building the road as I walked it, and I came into ministry at the same time, and the two callings have competed for the same finite hours of the same finite man every day for years. I know exactly what it is to give the best of my patience, my attention, my creativity, my emotional presence to the congregation, and to come home with the dregs, the tired and short version of myself, and to hand my sons the leftovers of a man the church got fresh. I am not describing a temptation I have observed in others. I am describing my own most persistent failure, and I name it because a chapter on this written from a posture of having solved it would be a lie, and you would smell the lie.

The lie the office tells is that the family will understand, that they are partners in the calling, that the sacrifice is shared and therefore holy. Sometimes it is shared, genuinely, and there is a real and beautiful thing where a family gives itself together to the work of God. But the line between a family that shares a calling and a family that is being consumed by a man's ambition is thin, and it is drawn in a place only the family can see, and the man at the center is the person least able to see it, because his vision is obstructed by the very thing he is sacrificing for. The children of pastors are a known wreckage in the church for a reason. Too many of them watched their father pour out on strangers a tenderness they themselves received only in exhausted fragments, and they concluded, not without evidence, that God was a thief who had stolen their father, and they walked away from the God who had taken him.

Eugene Peterson refused to let the pastoral vocation devour the ordinary, and he insisted that the pastor's own family and home and unspectacular daily faithfulness were not the part of his life he sacrificed for ministry but were themselves the soil of his ministry, the place his pastoring was either true or false before it was anything in public. A man who is gentle in the pulpit and harsh at his own table is not a gentle man who has a flaw at home. He is a harsh man who performs gentleness in public, and the public is being deceived, and the qualification "above reproach" has not been met, whatever the congregation believes.

Here is the verdict, and it is the hardest one in this book. A man who saves the world and loses his children has misunderstood both. He has misunderstood the world, because the world is not saved by his frantic over-functioning but by the God who does not need him to skip his son's life to accomplish His purposes. And he has misunderstood his children, because they were not an obstacle to his calling; they were, in part, his calling — the first and nearest flock, the one Scripture names explicitly, the one the church is told to watch as the proof of whether he can be trusted with any other. To say "I lost my family to the ministry" is not a tragic footnote to a faithful life. It is, by the standard of 1 Timothy 3, a disqualification dressed as a sacrifice.

I do not say this from above it. I say it from inside the daily fight not to do it. There are weeks I win and weeks I lose, and the weeks I lose look exactly like faithful ministry from the outside, which is precisely the danger. No one will ever rebuke a pastor for working too hard at the church. The board will praise him. The congregation will admire his dedication. The applause all runs one direction, toward the very imbalance that is hollowing out his home, and a man who needs applause — and which of us does not — will follow the applause, and the applause leads away from the door of his own house.

What does faithfulness look like? It looks like guarding the hours at home the way you guard your study time, refusing to apologize for them, treating your spouse and children as a real flock with a real claim and not as the support staff of your calling. It looks like making sure the man your family lives with is the man your congregation sees, and where he is not, fixing the man and not the performance. It looks like being willing, sometimes, to be a slightly less impressive pastor in order to be a present father, and trusting that the God who called you to the office also gave you the home, and is not asking you to destroy the one to serve the other. He never was. That was always the lie.
chapters.verdict: A man who saves the world and loses his children has misunderstood both the world and his children.
reflect: Does your family get your first energy or your leftovers?
Would your spouse and children describe the man at home as the man in the pulpit?
Whose approval are you working for when you stay late at the church?

chapters.title: Doubt in the Pulpit
chapters.summary: The pastor must proclaim certainties he sometimes does not feel; how to preach honestly through his own doubt without faking faith or contaminating the flock.
chapters.body:
There is a Sunday that comes to every honest pastor. He stands up to proclaim the resurrection, the love of God, the certainty of grace, and somewhere underneath the familiar words a cold voice asks whether any of it is true, and he has no answer ready, and he must preach anyway. The congregation needs the certainty. He does not, this morning, possess it. And he stands in the gap between what he is required to proclaim and what he can presently feel, and how he handles that gap will determine whether he is a man of integrity or a professional of religion. I came to faith out of atheism. I know the cold voice intimately. It did not die at my conversion. It learned to wait.

The church has handled pastoral doubt badly, mostly by pretending it does not exist. We have built a culture in which the pastor is the one person forbidden to wonder whether it is true, and so the doubt that visits him — and it visits everyone who thinks — has nowhere to go. He cannot voice it to the congregation; they need him solid. He often cannot voice it to other pastors; they are competitors in a culture of projected certainty. So he buries it, and buried doubt does not die. It goes underground and grows, and the man who could have walked through an honest season of questioning into a deeper faith instead lives a slow secret erosion behind a confident face, until one day the face and the man behind it have nothing left in common, and he is preaching a faith he privately abandoned years ago and cannot now afford to admit he abandoned.

Scripture is far more honest about this than the church is. The Psalms are full of men shouting accusations at God — "Why, O Lord, do you stand far away? Why do you hide yourself in times of trouble?" (Psalm 10:1). The God of the Bible apparently can absorb being yelled at; He preserved the yelling in His own book. John the Baptist, from prison, sent to ask whether Jesus was even the right man after all (Matthew 11:3) — John, who had baptized Him, who had seen the heavens open. If the forerunner could doubt the One he had pointed to, the pastor who has never doubted should ask whether he has ever genuinely engaged the questions or has simply never thought hard enough to find them. A faith that has never been tested is not strong. It is merely untried, and untried faith breaks the first time real weight comes down on it.

The cross itself contains the cry. "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46). The Son of God, in the hour of His deepest obedience, voicing abandonment. The church has spent two thousand years explaining that He was quoting a psalm, that He knew the resurrection was coming, that the abandonment was not real — and in our hurry to protect God from the appearance of doubt we have stripped the cry of the very thing that makes it the most comforting sentence in Scripture for the doubting believer. Whatever else it means, it means that the cry of abandonment is not outside the experience of God. He has been where you are on your worst Sunday. He is not scandalized by it. He spoke it Himself, from the cross, in the moment of His greatest faithfulness.

So how does an honest man preach through his own doubt without either faking a faith he does not feel or contaminating the flock with his unprocessed wrestling? The answer is not to perform a certainty he lacks; that is the lie that hollows him out. Nor is it to use the pulpit as his personal confessional, dumping his crisis onto people who came for bread; that is a different failure, the failure of a man who has confused honesty with self-indulgence and made the flock carry his weight. The answer is harder and quieter. He preaches the faith of the church, not the feeling of the moment. He proclaims what is true, not merely what he presently feels to be true, because the truth of the resurrection does not rise and fall with his Tuesday mood, and the congregation is entitled to the objective gospel and not to the subjective weather of his soul.

But — and this is the integrity that saves it — he takes the doubt itself somewhere real. He does not bury it. He brings it to God in private, to the few people who know the whole man, to honest books and honest prayer, and he lets it do its proper work, which is to drive shallow faith down toward bedrock. Doubt handled this way is not the enemy of faith; it is the plow that breaks up the hard ground of a faith grown merely habitual. The pastor who has walked through his own dark season and come out holding to God by his fingernails is a far better shepherd of the doubting than the man who has never wondered, because he can sit with the woman whose faith is collapsing and not be frightened by her questions, having survived his own.

"I believe; help my unbelief" (Mark 9:24). The man who said it was asking Jesus for a miracle and was honest enough to admit that his faith and his unbelief were occupying the same heart at the same moment. Jesus did not rebuke him. Jesus healed his son. That sentence is the truest thing most pastors could say about themselves on most days, and the freedom of the office begins the day a man stops pretending it is not true of him. Faith is not the absence of doubt. Faith is the direction a man faces while the doubt is still in the room.

I will not tell you I have conquered the cold voice. I will tell you I have learned to preach to it as well as past it, to let my own honest wrestling make my proclamation more true rather than less, because I am not standing up there pretending I never asked the hard question. I am standing up there as a man who asked it, who is still sometimes asking it, and who has nonetheless staked his life and his five sons' inheritance on the answer being yes. That is not the faith of a man who never doubted. It is the faith of a man who doubted and stayed. The congregation, more than they know, needs the second kind of man, because the second kind of man is the only one who can hold them when their own cold voice comes, as it surely will, on some Sunday of their own.
chapters.verdict: A pastor who has never doubted is either lying or has never thought hard enough to be trusted with anyone's faith.
reflect: Have you ever preached a confidence you did not feel that morning?
Where do you take your doubts, and is it anywhere at all?
Do you believe God can survive your honest questions?

chapters.title: Tending the Flock You Did Not Choose
chapters.summary: A pastor does not select his people; he is given them, including the difficult, the wounded, and the ones who will wound him, and the giving is the cost and the glory.
chapters.body:
A man does not choose his congregation. He is given one. This is among the hardest truths of the office, because everything in us wants to choose — to select the people who appreciate us, who follow easily, who do not drain us, who reflect well on our leadership. But the flock is given, not selected, and the giving includes the difficult, the chronically wounded, the perpetually offended, the slow, the demanding, and, eventually and inevitably, the ones who will turn on you and wound you deeply. To pastor is to love people you did not pick, cannot return, and sometimes cannot stand. That is not the obstacle to the calling. That is the calling.

The temptation is to pastor the congregation you wish you had rather than the one in front of you. The pastor builds, in his mind, an ideal church — responsive, growing, grateful, full of the kind of people he enjoys — and he begins, subtly, to resent the actual people for not being the ideal ones. He pours his energy into the promising and neglects the difficult. He preaches to the imagined responsive listener and grows cold toward the actual cranky one in the third row who has criticized his last six sermons. And in doing so he stops being a shepherd, because a shepherd is defined precisely by his commitment to the actual sheep, including the ones who wander and the ones who bite.

Jesus drew the line sharply: "The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees" (John 10:11-12). The difference between a shepherd and a hired hand is not skill. A hired hand can be very skilled. The difference is that the sheep belong to the shepherd, and so he stays when staying costs him, while the hired hand, who is in it for what he gets, leaves when the getting stops. The diagnostic is the wolf. When the difficult season comes — the conflict, the criticism, the season when the people are wounding rather than feeding you — does something in you rise to protect them, or does something in you calculate the exit? The wolf reveals which man you are. Everyone looks like a shepherd in the green pasture.

The people who wound you are the deepest test. Every pastor who stays long enough will be betrayed by someone he loved and served — an elder who turns, a family he poured years into who leaves bitter and tells a poisoned version of the story, a friend in the congregation who, in a conflict, chooses against him in a way that feels like having a knife slid between the ribs. And the temptation in the aftermath is to harden, to pull back, to never again give that much to anyone in the flock, to protect the soft places with a layer of professional distance. It is understandable. It is also the death of pastoral love, because a shepherd who has armored his heart against his sheep is no longer shepherding them; he is managing them from behind glass.

Christ tended a flock that abandoned Him, denied Him, and ran. He washed the feet of the man He knew would betray Him that very night (John 13). He did not pastor the disciples He wished He had. He pastored Peter, who would deny Him, and Thomas, who would doubt Him, and all of them, who would scatter. And after the resurrection He went and found Peter and restored him with a threefold "feed my sheep" (John 21:17), handing the man who had failed Him most spectacularly the very flock Christ was leaving behind. This is the pattern. The shepherd loves the sheep who fail him and entrusts the flock to the ones who wounded him, because the love is not contingent on the sheep deserving it. If it were, none of us would be in the flock at all.

I have been wounded by people I served and loved, and I will not pretend the wounds healed clean or that I have entirely forgiven where I should have. There are people who left my church with a story about me that I know to be false, and there is a part of me that wants to defend, to correct the record, to make sure the truth wins. The shepherd in me knows that I am to bless those who curse me and entrust the verdict to God. The man in me wants the verdict now and wants it in my favor. The gap between those two is where my own sanctification is being worked out in public, slowly, and not always toward the better.

There is glory in this, and I do not want to end only on the cost. To be given a people — actual people, with their actual histories and failures and the particular irreplaceable texture of their lives — and to be permitted to walk with them through births and deaths and the long ordinary middle, to be in the room for the worst day and the best one, to watch a difficult person you almost gave up on become, over a decade, soft and whole — there is no glory like it on the earth. The hired hand never knows this glory, because it is available only to the one who stayed, who loved the unlovely sheep, who did not flee when the wolf came. The cost and the glory are the same thing seen from two sides. You cannot have the second without paying the first.

"Shepherd the flock of God that is among you... not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples" (1 Peter 5:2-3). Among you. Not above. Not selected. Among. The flock God places among you is the only flock you will ever be judged for. Not the one you wanted. Not the one you could have built somewhere with better people. This one. These ones. The difficult man in the third row is not an obstacle to your ministry. He is your ministry, as much as anyone, and on the day you give an account, he will be standing there, and the question will not be how large your church grew or how well you preached. The question will be whether you loved him. You did not choose him. You were given him. That is the whole of it.
chapters.verdict: You will be judged not by the sheep you wanted but by the ones you were given.
reflect: Which person in your congregation are you secretly hoping leaves?
Do you love the people in front of you or the people you wish you had?
Are you a shepherd or a hired hand, and how would you know the difference?

chapters.title: The Account You Will Give
chapters.summary: Pastors will be judged more strictly; the office is held under the gaze of a final accounting that reframes every choice made in it.
chapters.body:
The verse we began with returns, and it is darker than we admitted. "Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness" (James 3:1). Greater strictness. The office is not only a weight in this life; it is a heightened liability in the next. The pastor handles holy things, speaks for God, shapes the eternal trajectory of souls, and he will answer for it under a standard higher than the one applied to the people he led. We have built a culture that treats ministry as a platform to ascend. James treats it as an account to render. These are opposite postures, and only one of them is sober.

The writer of Hebrews makes it concrete in the relationship between pastor and people: "Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account" (Hebrews 13:17). Keeping watch over souls. As those who will give an account. The pastor's authority and the pastor's accountability are the same coin. He has the weight of watching over souls precisely because he will answer for how he watched. Strip out the accounting and the authority becomes mere power, which is what we too often see. Keep the accounting in view and the authority becomes what it was meant to be: a terrifying stewardship held by a man who knows he will stand before the Owner and explain what he did with what he was given.

Imagine the account honestly. Not the version where you list your sermons preached and your church's attendance and your books published. The real one, where the Lord who sees the heart asks not what you did but why, and the motives you successfully hid from your congregation and half-hid from yourself are laid out in the light. The growth you pursued — for the kingdom, or for your name? The hard truths you withheld — out of love, or out of cowardice dressed as love? The difficult member you avoided, the family you neglected at home, the doubt you buried rather than brought to God, the gift you turned into an idol, the gap you let widen between the public man and the private one. Every chapter of this book is a line item in that account. The accounting is not an abstraction I am adding for solemnity. It is the actual frame within which the whole office is held, and the man who forgets it is the man most likely to fail it.

This is not meant to crush. It is meant to clarify. There is a strange freedom in the final accounting, because it relocates the verdict that matters. The pastor lives under a thousand smaller verdicts — the congregation's approval, the board's assessment, the comparison with the church down the road, the reviews of his preaching, the number in the seats. These verdicts are constant, contradictory, and exhausting, and a man who lives for them will be torn apart by them, because they can never all be satisfied and they shift with every season. The final accounting silences them. There is one verdict that matters, rendered by One who sees the whole truth, and a man who lives for that verdict is freed from the tyranny of all the smaller ones. He can disappoint the congregation to please the Lord. He can refuse the growth that would have enlarged him. He can love the difficult sheep no one praises him for loving, because the praise was never the point; the account was.

Paul lived this way with a clarity that should provoke us. "With me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court... It is the Lord who judges me" (1 Corinthians 4:3-4). A very small thing. The opinions that consume most pastors, Paul calls a very small thing, because his eyes were fixed on the only court whose verdict was final. And then, the sentence that should be tattooed on the inside of every pastor's eyelids: "Do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart" (1 Corinthians 4:5). The purposes of the heart. That is what the account is about. Not the visible work. The hidden purposes underneath it, which God will disclose, and which we spend our whole ministries either tending or hiding.

I think about my account. I think about it more as I get older and the proportion of ministry behind me grows against the proportion ahead. I think about my five sons standing in their own accounts someday and what I will have to answer for in how I fathered them while I pastored. I think about the people I served well and the people I failed, the motives I am proud of and the ones I would give a great deal to have purified before they are disclosed. I am not writing this chapter from a settled peace about my own account. I am writing it from the holy unease that the account is real, that it is coming, and that it is the truest thing about the office, truer than any of the metrics we use to measure ourselves in the meantime.

Bonhoeffer walked to his execution at Flossenbürg in April 1945 having staked everything on the reality that there is a verdict beyond the verdicts of men, that the regime that was about to hang him did not hold the final account, that the One who did held it differently than the world could imagine. He had written that costly grace is the gospel which must be sought again and again, the call which must be obeyed, the only grace worth having. A man who knows he will give an account holds his ministry as costly grace — received freely, held under judgment, spent for the One who will assess it. The hireling has no account; he has only wages, paid now, spent now, gone. The shepherd has an account, and it reframes everything, and it is the soberest and finally the most freeing truth the office contains.

You are not building a ministry. You thought you were. You are preparing to give an account. Hold every choice in that light, and the choices clarify. Forget it, and you will spend your life impressing a court that does not matter while neglecting the One that does.
chapters.verdict: You are not building a ministry. You are preparing to give an account.
reflect: If you gave your account today, what would you be ashamed had been your real motives?
Are you living for the verdict of your congregation or of your Lord?
Whom are you neglecting that the final accounting will ask you about?

chapters.title: Worth Everything
chapters.summary: After ten chapters of cost and warning, the case that the calling rightly held and rightly counted is worth more than anything surrendered for it.
chapters.body:
I have spent ten chapters telling you why most people should not do this. I have set down the weight, closed the door on those it would crush, screened for the character we ignore, named the temptations the office breeds, exposed the loneliness and the idolatry and the cost to the family and the strictness of the final account. If you have read this far and the calling has died in you under the weight of it, then this book has done its kindest work, and you should walk away with my blessing and no shame. But if you have read this far and the calling is still there — quieter now, stripped of its romance, sobered and frightened but not gone — then I owe you the last word, which is the truest one. It is worth everything. It is worth all of it.

Not because the costs were exaggerated. They were not. Every one is real and you will pay every one. It is worth everything for the same reason the pearl of great price was worth everything to the merchant who sold all he had to buy it (Matthew 13:45-46) — not because the cost was small, but because the thing obtained was beyond all comparison with the cost. The merchant did not get a bargain. He gave everything. And he counted it gain, because what he received was worth more than everything he gave, and he knew it, and the giving was not loss but the truest profit of his life. That is the structure of this calling for the one truly given to it. You will give everything. You will count it gain.

What is the everything you receive? Let me name what I have actually tasted, beneath the cost, in fifteen years of this work. I have been in the room when a man who came to me an atheist — as I once was — closed his eyes and crossed over into faith, and I have watched the thing happen to a human soul that happened to mine, and there is no glory on the earth like being present at a resurrection. I have held the hands of the dying and watched some of them go out not in terror but in a peace that the world cannot manufacture and cannot explain, and I have known, standing there, that what I gave them across the years was not platitudes but the one thing that holds at the edge. I have watched marriages that should have ended grow old and tender. I have buried the saints and felt, at the graveside, not only grief but a strange fierce hope that I did not put there and could not fake.

These are not the byproducts of the calling. They are the calling. The cost is the entry fee; this is what is purchased. And the one truly called is the one for whom this exchange is not a hard bargain but the deepest desire of his heart — who would, if he were honest, pay it all again, who finds in the giving of himself to these people the very thing his soul was made for, who discovers that the weight he was warned about is, when carried by the man built to carry it, not a burden but a kind of home. "My yoke is easy, and my burden is light" (Matthew 11:30) — and the paradox is that the same yoke that crushes the wrong man fits the called man so well that he can hardly imagine living without it.

This is the final test, and it is gentler than the others and more revealing. If you laid the office down tomorrow — walked away clean, with honor, no scandal, simply set it down — would your soul be relieved or bereft? The man who is not called would be relieved, finally, of a weight that never fit him, and that relief is a mercy and a sign and he should heed it. The man who is called would be bereft, would feel an amputation, would discover that the thing he had been complaining about carrying was the thing his life was wrapped around, and he would not know who he was without it. Not because the gift had become his idol — we covered that danger — but because the calling had become his obedience, and to lay down a true obedience is to lose, for a moment, the thread of why God made you. The relieved man should go in peace. The bereft man has his answer.

Paul, at the end, in a Roman cell, wrote the sentence that every pastor hopes to be able to mean when his own end comes: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith" (2 Timothy 4:7). He did not write that he had built a great ministry or grown a large church or achieved renown. He wrote that he had fought, finished, and kept — the language of a soldier and a runner and a steward, not a celebrity. And he wrote it from prison, near death, having lost by every worldly measure, and it is the most triumphant sentence in his letters, because he was measuring by the only account that mattered, and by that account he had won everything, having given everything.

I came to this God from atheism, with no father to show me what a steady man looked like, with nothing that recommended me for the care of souls. By every reasonable standard I should not be holding this office. That I am holding it is not a credit to me; it is the strangeness of a God who calls the unlikely and then, having called them, makes them able. If He could call me, the warning of this book stands and so does its hope. Most should not enter. Some are made for it. The difference is not talent or pedigree or even desire. The difference is the call — the weight laid on a man by God, which he can no more shake off than he can shake off his own name.

So here is the last word, and I leave it as weight, not resolution. If God has not called you, this office will be the slow undoing of your soul, and the door that closed to you was love. If God has called you, it will cost you everything you have and everything you are, and you will stand at the end like Paul, having lost by the world's measure and won by the only one that holds, and you will say, with your last honest breath, that it was worth all of it. Count the cost. Then, if you still must — only if you still must — pick up the weight.
chapters.verdict: The calling will cost you everything, and for the one truly called, it is the only thing worth the price.
reflect: Knowing now what it costs, do you still want it, or are you finally free to want it rightly?
What is the glory you have actually tasted in this work, beneath the cost?
If you laid the office down tomorrow, would your soul be relieved or bereft?
